claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are equiatomic random solid solutions.
Local copper segregation to nanoparticle surfaces governs the onset of premelting and melting.
Surface copper enrichment reduces local cohesive bonding.
Reduced local cohesive bonding caused by copper enrichment initiates melting at lower temperatures than in chemically homogeneous particles.
Changing cooling rate can alter atomic mobility and thereby promote or suppress copper surface segregation.
An inert or high-vacuum atmosphere prevents oxidation during heating.
Holding nanoparticle size constant isolates the effect of chemical ordering on thermal behavior.
Chemical short-range-order fluctuations lead to copper enrichment at interfaces and surface facets.
Heating mobilizes atoms in the nanoparticles.
Differences in atomic size and bonding energies cause copper to segregate preferentially to the nanoparticle surface.
Copper has a lower melting point and reduced cohesive energy relative to the other Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu constituents.
Copper-rich, weakly bonded surface regions act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles undergo pronounced surface premelting below the bulk melting point.
Particles with greater surface copper segregation will have lower premelting and melting onset temperatures than more compositionally homogeneous particles.
Rapid cooling locks in a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Rapidly cooled homogeneous particles will have higher premelting and melting temperatures and more uniform melting behavior.
Surface-to-volume effects are significant for nanoparticles below tens of nanometers.
The proposed mechanism is most applicable when constituent elements differ substantially in melting point and cohesive energy.
